# International rental property for a US investor

Nine countries — Costa Rica, Hungary, France, Spain, Italy, Portugal, Greece,
Mexico, Panama — assessed for a US-resident investor buying residential property
to rent out, long-term or short-term.

Supporting detail is in [references/](references/); every source is numbered in
[citations.md](citations.md).

---

## 1. Limitations — read before the findings

This study answers the **legal and regulatory** half of the question well and the
**financial** half barely at all. Stating that first, because the shape of the
gaps determines what the document can be used for.

**1.1 Search ran on one engine.** The sanctioned multi-engine path had exactly
one usable web backend alive for the whole run, so no query could form the two
independent waves the method depends on. Of **102 queries**, **94 report
`single_wave: true`** and the remaining **8 returned no results at all** — those
report `single_wave: false` only because no wave succeeded, which is the
zero-wave case, not a second sample. The pool is **641 unique URLs**. Roughly 85%
of search results are unique to a single engine, so this pool is materially
narrower than the method assumes — the skill's own methodology basis puts about
85% of search results as unique to a single engine, which is why the multi-engine
path exists. **Absence of a source in this study is weak evidence that the source
does not exist.**

**1.2 No yield, anywhere.** There is no gross rental yield, price-to-rent ratio,
or days-on-market figure for any of the nine countries in this corpus, and none
for the United States. **The central comparison the question implies — is this
better than buying at home — cannot be made from this evidence base, in either
direction.**

**1.3 No price-per-square-foot conversion is published.** The user's baseline is
US cost per square foot. Converting a European €/m² figure requires knowing the
measured-area basis — France's *loi Carrez*, Spain's *superficie útil* versus
*construida*, Italy's *superficie commerciale* — and **no fetched source
establishes the basis for any price series**. The arithmetic is trivial; the
like-for-like comparison is not, so the conversion is withheld rather than
published with a false precision.

**1.4 Six of nine countries have no price or rent level at all.** Only Hungary
and Mexico have usable figures, plus one region-level figure for France. The
Paris-versus-countryside split the user specifically asked about is **not met**,
for France.

**1.5 Round-trip transaction cost is not computable for any country.** Two of
nine have a sourced acquisition tax rate. None has a notary tariff, registry fee,
agent commission, or annual property tax rate.

**1.6 Three cost lines that block a net-yield model are effectively absent**:
long-term management fees and landlord insurance for all nine countries, and any
observed maintenance figure for eight of nine — the sole exception being French
co-ownership charges, reported second-hand as an average rising from €1,886/year
in 2021 to €2,259/year in 2024 [30]. Three tax-deduction conventions in the corpus
(Costa Rica's deemed 15%, Hungary's flat 10%, Italy's 5%) are **not** maintenance
estimates and are not used as such.

**1.7 A whole risk dimension was lost to source failure.** Every US State
Department Investment Climate Statement returned an error body, and the IMF's
exchange-restrictions register refused the retrieval path. Consequence: **no
expropriation record, no investor-state case count, no capital-control evidence
and no investment-treaty recourse evidence for any of the nine.**

**1.8 Retrieval failed on 47 of 204 fetches (23%)** — within the expected band,
but concentrated: every Greek tax-authority source, every Mexico City short-let
source, Panama's official gazette, Spain's housing ministry, and CEPEJ.

---

## 2. What the study does establish

Six findings are well sourced from primary text and would survive audit.

**2.1 Six of the nine countries have no US estate tax treaty.** France, Italy and
Greece do; **Costa Rica, Hungary, Spain, Portugal, Mexico and Panama do not**
[45][46]. Without a treaty a US decedent's foreign real property can be taxed in
both jurisdictions, and the fallback IRC § 2014 credit is narrow — two ratio
limits, no credit for interest or penalties, a four-year claim window, refunds
without interest [49][51]. This is the single most decision-relevant finding in
the study and it was previously confirmed for France only.

**2.2 Spain taxes a US landlord on gross rent.** 24% for third-country residents
against 19% for EU/EEA, and — the part that matters more — expense deduction is
available **only** to EU/EEA residents [37]. An EU owner pays 19% on net; a US
owner pays 24% on gross. On a 30% cost ratio the effective burden is roughly
13.3% versus 24%, about **1.8×**, not the 1.26× the headline rates suggest.

**2.3 Portugal's non-resident IMT surcharge is real, and the date confusion is
explained.** CIMT art. 17(10), added by DL 97/2026 of 20 May 2026, sets a flat
**7.5%** with all reliefs disapplied for non-resident buyers of urban residential
property [9][10]. The competing "1 September 2026" claim in circulation attaches
to *other* provisions of the same decree — the DL 68/2019 revocation, the CIA
regime and the RSAA — and **not** to the IMT article, which Article 18 never
names. The rate and the diploma are sourced; **the commencement date is not
stated in the primary and is not asserted here**.

**2.4 Two countries gate a US buyer at the door.** Hungary requires a
**discretionary per-property permit**, HUF 65,000, 45-day deadline, with mandatory
refusal where public or municipal interest is harmed [3][4]; the US is on no
exemption list. Mexico bars direct title in the restricted zone — 100 km from
borders, 50 km from coasts — allowing only a 50-year bank trust conferring use
and enjoyment "sin constituir derechos reales sobre ellos" [5][6].

**2.5 Costa Rica's coast is closed, by statute.** Ley 6043 art. 47 bars
concessions to foreigners without five years' residence, to entities domiciled
abroad, to entities formed in Costa Rica by foreigners, and to entities more than
50% foreign-owned, voiding breaching transfers [7]. This is a bar, not a permit.

**2.6 Short-term rental rules are moving against the non-resident letting
investor, fast.** Barcelona extinguishes every tourist-flat licence by November
2028 [17][18]; Greece freezes new central-Athens registrations to 31 December
2026 **and deletes the registration on any sale** [25]; Spain's national registry
was annulled by the Supreme Court within 18 months [15][16]; Italy cut the
short-let volume ceiling from four apartments to two from 2026 [28]; Portugal has
rewritten the regime roughly every two years [20][21].

### 3.5 Civil justice speed — a proxy, not an eviction time

Estimated days to resolve litigious civil and commercial cases at first instance,
2022 [32]: **Hungary 134 · Portugal 238 · France 333 · Spain 359 · Italy 540 ·
Greece 746**. Not eviction-specific, calculated rather than measured, and see
[tenancy-law.md](references/tenancy-law.md) for the extraction caveat. Costa
Rica, Mexico and Panama are not covered by any equivalent.

Only France has a possession-recovery figure: an **8-month incompressible
minimum**, often "closer to two years" in practice [30].

## 4. Per-country summary

**Hungary** — the only country with both a documented entry gate and good price
data. Permit at HUF 65,000 per property, 45 days, refusable on municipal
interest [3][4]. Transfer duty 4% to HUF 1bn, 2% above, capped at HUF 200m [12].
Prime-to-rural price spread 2.87× [54]. Fastest civil courts in the EU and 22nd
of 27 on perceived judicial independence [33] — a divergence worth weighing. **No
US estate tax treaty, and the income tax treaty is terminated** [45][50].

**Spain** — the worst tax base for a US owner of the nine that were sourced: 24%
on gross with no deductions [37]. Barcelona is removing an entire licence class
by 2028 [17][18]. National short-let registry annulled mid-2026, replacement
unknown [16]. No estate tax treaty. No price or rent level retrieved.

**Portugal** — a quantified 7.5% entry penalty on non-residents, with a lawful
escape that requires accepting a capped rent for at least 36 months in five years
[9][10]. The 2023 short-let freeze was repealed, but a condominium can veto AL
registration by two-thirds permilage, and the licence is non-transferable [21].
Mid-pack courts, 24th of 27 on *company* perceived independence [33]. No estate
tax treaty. Rental income taxed at a **25% autonomous rate** [21], with a
duration-keyed reduction ladder for longer leases, and **no option to aggregate**
— that is residents-only [44].

**France** — the only country with real possession-recovery data, and it is
unfavourable: 8 months minimum, ~2 years in practice, 30,500 evictions executed
in 2025 [30]. Paris caps principal-residence letting at **90 nights** and requires
change-of-use *with compensation* for anything else [24] — a capital barrier for
a non-resident. **The only country of the nine with both estate and gift tax
treaties** [45]. But: no acquisition-rights source, no tax rate, and no rural
price figure.

**Italy** — CIN regime in force since 2 November 2024 with three stacked
registration layers and per-violation fines [22][23]; the short-let volume ceiling
fell to two apartments from 2026 [28]. **27th of 27 on civil and commercial
disposition time across all court instances** in 2023 [33] — note this is the
all-instances measure; on the 2022 first-instance measure Italy is at 540 days
and Greece is slower at 746 [32]. Has an estate tax treaty [45]. On acquisition, **the 1949 US–Italy Treaty of
Friendship, Commerce and Navigation grants US citizens national treatment on
immovable property** [8]; whether Italy's foreign ministry treats that as
discharging the Art. 16 reciprocity condition is unconfirmed, since its country
list is blocked [1][2]. Whether a non-resident may elect the 21% flat tax is also
unestablished [29].

**Greece** — one strong finding and otherwise a blank. Central Athens is frozen
to new short-let registrations, and **a sale deletes an existing registration**
[25]. Has an estate tax treaty [45]. **Nominal** rents fell 16% between 2010 and
2024 — the only EU country to decline in nominal terms, against cumulative Greek
inflation of 20% over the same period, so the real-terms fall is steeper still
[59]. Housing cost overburden is the EU's highest at 29% in cities. 26th of 27 on
investment-protection confidence [33]. Every tax-authority source was
inaccessible [64].

**Mexico** — best-documented ownership structure of the nine, and the most
structurally constrained on the coast: a 50-year trust with no rights in rem, a
discretionary standard, and a fine up to the full transaction value for
circumvention [5][6]. 25% on gross rent, with a **US-resident-specific**
net-basis election that must be filed every January–February [39][40]. No estate
tax treaty. Short-let regulation entirely unsourced [67].

**Costa Rica** — the coast and all islands are barred to a non-resident by
statute [7]; the inland regime is unevidenced. Cleanest exit arithmetic of the
Latin American three: 15% on rent after a deemed 15% allowance, 15% on gains, 2.5%
buyer withholding on sale by a non-domiciled owner [14]. National ICT short-let
registration with no caps found [27]. No estate tax treaty; no price data; no
court-duration data.

**Panama** — the weakest evidence base of the nine. Nothing establishes who may
buy or under what instrument [68]. Rental income rate not established [41]. Long
leases escape ITBMS where the term exceeds six months [42]. Possession recovery is
administrative through MIVIOT rather than judicial [36]. Sub-investment-grade
from one rating agency since March 2024, debt ~70% of GDP, and an official summary
naming "non-payment issues" and weak judicial capacity as impediments [62].

## 5. Contradictions surfaced rather than resolved

Recorded because the reader needs to see them.

1. **Portugal IMT commencement.** Secondary sources split 25 May vs 1 September
   2026. The primary shows the 1 September date belongs to other provisions of the
   same decree; the IMT article's commencement is simply not stated [9][10].
2. **Portugal AL registration period.** Turismo de Portugal says 60 and 90
   **working** days; gov.pt says 60 and 90 days [19][20]. Both are official.
3. **Spain RD 1312/2024 effects date.** The operative clause says 1 July 2025;
   the BOE's own metadata block on the same page says 1 June 2025 [15].
4. **Portugal CIMT amendment list.** The tax authority's page annotates art.
   17(10) as added by DL 97/2026 while its "Artigo alterado por" list omits that
   diploma [9].
5. **CGPJ press note.** Its subtitle presents shares as year-on-year changes; the
   body figures are the correct ones [31].
6. **Two Portuguese rent ceilings that look like one.** DL 97/2026 art. 2(2)(a)
   sets 2.5× the minimum monthly wage as the cap gating the IMT escape; the RSAA
   in annex iii of the same decree sets 80% of the INE median rent for the
   concelho for its own exemption. Both are in the decree and they are not the
   same number [10].
7. **CEPEJ day counts.** One analysis pass cross-validated the values against a
   second figure in the same document; another noted the mapping was inferred from
   an ascending series. Ordinal ranking is safe; the day counts should be
   re-verified [32].

## 6. Decision framework

Given what is and is not established, the order of questions that actually
discriminates between these nine:

1. **Can you buy at all, and what do you own?** Rule out on tenure before
   anything else. Costa Rica's coast is barred [7]; Mexico's restricted zone gives
   you a trust, not title [5]; Hungary needs a refusable permit [3]; Italy is
   unresolved [1][2].
2. **What happens on death?** Six of nine have no US estate tax treaty
   [45][46]. If the property is meant to pass to heirs, this eliminates more
   candidates than any other single test, and it is cheap to check.
3. **What is the tax base, not the tax rate?** Spain's 24%-on-gross and Mexico's
   25%-on-gross are worse than their headline rates imply [37][39]. Ask whether
   expenses are deductible before comparing percentages.
4. **Does your rental strategy survive the regulator?** If the plan is short-let,
   Barcelona, central Athens and Paris are each documented as hostile in a
   different way, and Greece's transfer-deletion rule specifically penalises a
   buyer [17][25][24].
5. **How long to recover possession?** Only France has a figure, and it is 8
   months minimum and about two years in practice [30]. Elsewhere, use the civil
   disposition-time proxy [32] and label it as a proxy.
6. **Then, and only then, the numbers** — which this study cannot give you. Any
   yield model needs management fees, insurance, maintenance, vacancy and a
   measured-area basis, none of which this run sourced for any country.

**The honest summary:** on this evidence, the countries separate cleanly on
*legal* grounds and not at all on *financial* grounds. A reader can use this
document to eliminate candidates and to avoid specific traps. A reader cannot use
it to decide whether any of the nine beats a US-domestic rental, because nothing
here measures that.
